He returned to Nigeria in the 1980s and was employed by [Mobil Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobil "Mobil") as an accountant, before entering politics as a Lagos West senatorial candidate in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Nigerian_Senate_elections_in_Lagos_State#Lagos_West "1992 Nigerian Senate elections in Lagos State") under the banner of the [Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_(Nigeria) "Social Democratic Party (Nigeria)"). After the military dictator [Sani Abacha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sani_Abacha "Sani Abacha") dissolved the Senate in 1993, Tinubu went into exile and became an activist campaigning for the return of democracy as a part of the [National Democratic Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Coalition_(Nigeria) "National Democratic Coalition (Nigeria)") movement.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

In the [first post-transition Lagos State gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Lagos_State_gubernatorial_election "1999 Lagos State gubernatorial election"), Tinubu won by a wide margin as a member of the [Alliance for Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_for_Democracy_(Nigeria) "Alliance for Democracy (Nigeria)"). Four years later, he won re-election to a second term. After leaving office in 2007, he played a key role in forming the [All Progressives Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Progressives_Congress "All Progressives Congress") in 2013. In 2023, he was [elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerian_presidential_election "2023 Nigerian presidential election") president, defeating [Atiku Abubakar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiku_Abubakar "Atiku Abubakar") and [Peter Obi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Obi "Peter Obi").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Under his leadership the government ended prior [fuel subsidies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_subsidies "Fuel subsidies"), citing fiscal pressures,[[5]](#cite_note-5) dissolved the governing boards of numerous federal agencies and state-owned enterprises, replaced the majority of military and paramilitary leadership, supported regional efforts to respond to the [2025 Benin coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Benin_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2025 Benin coup d'état") while engaging with [security cooperation with the United States against the Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_United_States_strikes_in_Nigeria "2025 United States strikes in Nigeria") and survived an alleged coup attempt.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

## Early life

Tinubu was born in Lagos to a Muslim family from the [Yoruba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_people "Yoruba people") ethnic group,[[8]](#cite_note-8) the son of [Abibatu Mogaji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abibatu_Mogaji "Abibatu Mogaji"), the [Ìyál'ọ́jà](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Cy%C3%A1l'%E1%BB%8D%CC%81j%C3%A0 "Ìyál'ọ́jà") of [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"). He is generally accepted in reliable sources to have been born in 1952;[[9]](#cite_note-9) this year of birth is sometimes disputed by political opponents, who argue that he is much older. Some reliable sources note that his age has not been verified.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

### Education

Tinubu attended St. John's Primary School, Aroloya, Lagos before proceeding to Children Home School in [Ibadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibadan "Ibadan").[[12]](#cite_note-12) Tinubu arrived in the United States in 1975, where he commenced undergraduate studies first at [Richard J. Daley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley_College "Richard J. Daley College") in Chicago and then at [Chicago State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_State_University "Chicago State University") where he majored in [accounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accounting "Accounting") and [management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Management "Management"). He worked odd jobs as a dishwasher, night security guard and cab driver to support himself through college.[[13]](#cite_note-asiwajubolatinubu_2011-07-23-13) He made the honor [dean's list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean's_list "Dean's list") as an undergraduate and taught remedial class tutorials, some of his classmates credited his lectures for their improved grades. Tinubu was the university accounting society president in his senior year. His cumulative GPA was 3.54.[[13]](#cite_note-asiwajubolatinubu_2011-07-23-13) Tinubu graduated [summa cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_cum_laude "Summa cum laude") with a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration in 1979.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Niger is a member of [ECOWAS](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS "ECOWAS"), which has already suspended [Guinea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinea "Guinea"), [Mali](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali") and [Burkina Faso](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burkina_Faso "Burkina Faso") from membership due to successful coups in recent years. On 26 July 2023, [a coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerien_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2023 Nigerien coup d'état") occurred in [Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger "Niger"), during which the country's presidential guard removed and detained president [Mohamed Bazoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bazoum "Mohamed Bazoum"). Subsequently, General [Abdourahamane Tchiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdourahamane_Tchiani "Abdourahamane Tchiani"), the Commander of the Presidential Guard, proclaimed himself the leader of the country and established the [National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_the_Safeguard_of_the_Homeland "National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland"), after confirming the success of the coup.[[5]](#cite_note-7)[[6]](#cite_note-8)[[7]](#cite_note-9)[[8]](#cite_note-ajtchiani-10)

In response to this development, the [Economic Community of West African States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS "ECOWAS") (ECOWAS) issued an ultimatum on 30 July, giving the coup leaders in Niger one week to reinstate Bazoum, with the threat of [international sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions "International sanctions") and potential [use of force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi

ki/Use_of_force "Use of force").[[9]](#cite_note-11)[[10]](#cite_note-12) When the deadline of the ultimatum expired on 6 August, no military intervention was initiated; however, on 10 August, ECOWAS took the step of activating its standby force.[[11]](#cite_note-NC-13)[[12]](#cite_note-BE-14)[[13]](#cite_note-DS-15)[[14]](#cite_note-EL-16) Previously in 2017, ECOWAS had launched a [military intervention to restore democracy in The Gambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS_military_intervention_in_the_Gambia "ECOWAS military intervention in the Gambia") during a [constitutional crisis within the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%932017_Gambian_constitutional_crisis "2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis").

All active member states of ECOWAS, except for Cape Verde, pledged to engage their armed forces in the event of an ECOWAS-led military intervention against the Nigerien junta.[[15]](#cite_note-17) Conversely, the military juntas in Burkina Faso and Mali announced they would send troops in support of the junta were such a military intervention launched while [forming a mutual defense pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Sahel_States "Alliance of Sahel States").[[16]](#cite_note-18)[[17]](#cite_note-PO-19)

On 24 February 2024, ECOWAS announced that it was lifting sanctions on Niger, purportedly for [humanitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarianism "Humanitarianism") purposes.[[1]](#cite_note-WA-1)

On 26 July 2023, President [Mohamed Bazoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bazoum "Mohamed Bazoum"), [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_Niger "First Lady of Niger") [Hadiza Bazoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadiza_Bazoum "Hadiza Bazoum"), and their son, Salem Bazoum, were detained at the [Presidential Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Palace,_Niamey "Presidential Palace, Niamey") in [Niamey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niamey "Niamey"), and Interior Minister [Hamadou Souley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamadou_Souley "Hamadou Souley") was also arrested. The coup was led by General [Abdourahamane Tchiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdourahamane_Tchiani "Abdourahamane Tchiani"), whom Bazoum had planned to relieve from his position.[[18]](#cite_note-20)[[19]](#cite_note-21)[[20]](#cite_note-NS-22)[[21]](#cite_note-23)[[22]](#cite_note-24) In the evening, [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_of_Niger "Air Force of Niger") Colonel-Major [Amadou Abdramane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadou_Abdramane "Amadou Abdramane") announced on state television that Bazoum had been removed from power and announced the formation of a [National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_the_Safeguard_of_the_Homeland "National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland"), dissolution of the country's Constitution, the suspension of all state institutions, the closure of borders, and a nationwide curfew from 22:00 until 05:00 local time, while warning against any foreign intervention.[[20]](#cite_note-NS-22)[[23]](#cite_note-25)[[24]](#cite_note-26) Subsequently, all activities by [political parties in the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Niger "List of political parties in Niger") were ordered suspended until further notice.[[25]](#cite_note-27)

Despite his detention, Bazoum has so far refused to resign.[[26]](#cite_note-bbc2-28) While declaring himself acting head of state and calling for resistance against the coup,[[26]](#cite_note-bbc2-28) Bazoum's Foreign Minister [Hassoumi Massaoudou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassoumi_Massaoudou "Hassoumi Massaoudou") told [France 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_24 "France 24") that the country's "legal and legitimate power" remained with the President.[[27]](#cite_note-29) However, the leadership of the Nigerien armed forces declared its support for the coup to protect the President and avoid "a deadly confrontation."[[28]](#cite_note-30)

On 28 July, Tchiani proclaimed himself as the president of the junta, saying that he had deposed Bazoum to avoid "the gradual and inevitable demise" of the country and accusing him of covering up the country's situation. Tchiani did not give a timeline for a return to civilian rule.[[29]](#cite_note-f24tchiani-31)[[30]](#cite_note-32)[[8]](#cite_note-ajtchiani-10)

The [Economic Community of West African States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Community_of_West_African_States "Economic Community of West African States") (ECOWAS) is a regional, political and economic union of fifteen countries in West Africa, covering an area of 5,114,162 km2 (1,974,589 sq mi) and with an estimated population of over 387 million in 2019. Established in 1975, ECOWAS aims to achieve collective self-sufficiency for its member states by creating a single large trade bloc.[[31]](#cite_note-33)[[32]](#cite_note-34)

ECOWAS also serves as a [peacekeeping](http

The United States, France, and many other countries and groups have been involved in [Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger "Niger") because of the [Islamist insurgency in the Sahel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamist_insurgency_in_the_Sahel "Islamist insurgency in the Sahel"), which in turn triggered the [Jihadist insurgency in Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jihadist_insurgency_in_Niger "Jihadist insurgency in Niger") led by [Al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda"), the [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") group and [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram").[[36]](#cite_note-38)[[37]](#cite_note-39)[[38]](#cite_note-40)[[39]](#cite_note-41) The United States, France, and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") have had bases in the country. In 2022, it became a hub of French anti-terror operations after its departure from [Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali") and [Burkina Faso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burkina_Faso "Burkina Faso") following a series of military coups[[40]](#cite_note-42) and [anti-French sentiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-French_sentiment "Anti-French sentiment") which paved the way for Russian influence and the entry of its private mercenary firm [Wagner Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagner_Group "Wagner Group") in the region.[[41]](#cite_note-43)[*[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*] At the same time, it paved the way for Turkish influence in the region.[[42]](#cite_note-44)[[43]](#cite_note-45)[[44]](#cite_note-46)

The military junta accused ECOWAS in a statement read by Abdramane on [Télé Sahel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%A9l%C3%A9_Sahel "Télé Sahel") of planning to approve "a plan of aggression against Niger through an imminent military intervention in Niamey supported by certain Western countries" and warned of the junta's "strong determination" to defend the country. They claimed that this was the objective of the ECOWAS summit convened for the following day.[[45]](#cite_note-47)

The [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union") Peace and Security Council issued an ultimatum that if the soldiers did not "immediately and unconditionally return to their barracks and restore constitutional democracy, within a maximum of fifteen days" that the bloc would be compelled to take "necessary action, including punitive measures against perpetrators".[[46]](#cite_note-48)

Members of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") strongly condemned the coup and expressed support for ECOWAS and the AU.[[47]](#cite_note-49)

##### ECOWAS ultimatum and sanctions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nigerien_crisis_(2023%E2%80%932024)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: ECOWAS ultimatum and sanctions")]

On 30 July, ECOWAS issued the Nigerien military junta with an ultimatum that Bazoum be reinstated as president within one week. In a communiqué read by ECOWAS Commission chairperson [Omar Touray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Touray "Omar Touray"), at the Extraordinary Summit convened in [Abuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja"), Nigeria in response to the coup, they said that if their demands were not met they would "take all measures necessary to restore constitutional order" in Niger and that "such measures may include the use of force".[[48]](#cite_note-50)[[49]](#cite_note-51) The response from the bloc towards the junta drastically differed from the measures taken with recent coups in [Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Malian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2021 Malian

ECOWAS also announced "immediate sanctions" on Niger, including the closure of land and air borders, imposition of a [no-fly zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-fly_zone "No-fly zone") on all commercial flights to and from Niger and the suspension of all commercial and financial transactions between ECOWAS and Niger.[[51]](#cite_note-Balima-53) The assets of Niger state enterprises were frozen by the ECOWAS Central Bank, leading to the cancellation of a 30 billion CFA francs ($51 million) bond issuance.[[52]](#cite_note-54) ECOWAS also cut off more than 70% of Niger's electricity supply.[[53]](#cite_note-55) The sanctions included a sizable ban on goods such as food, pharmaceuticals, medical equipment, petroleum, and electricity. ECOWAS also cut off more than 70% of Niger's electricity supply. However, Mali and Burkina Faso did not implement ECOWAS sanctions on Niger. [[54]](#cite_note-:0-56)

##### Pro-coup demonstrations in Niamey

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nigerien_crisis_(2023%E2%80%932024)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Pro-coup demonstrations in Niamey")]

In a march at the request of Tchiani and organized by the [M62 Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M62_Movement "M62 Movement"), which had previously opposed Bazoum's government and [Operation Barkhane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barkhane "Operation Barkhane") and supported the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine"), thousands of pro-coup Nigeriens gathered in Niamey's Place de la Concertation, in front of the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(Niger) "National Assembly (Niger)"), and went to the French Embassy carrying Nigerien, Russian and North Korean flags, with slogans such as "Down with France, out with Barkhane, we don't care about ECOWAS, the European Union and the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union")!", "Arrest the former dignitaries to return the stolen millions.", and "Down with France, long live [Putin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin")!".[[55]](#cite_note-PP-57)[[56]](#cite_note-FR-58)[[50]](#cite_note-RF-52)[[57]](#cite_note-59) The demonstrators also called for an immediate intervention by the Wagner Group.[[56]](#cite_note-FR-58) During the march, the entrances to the French and American embassies were closed.[[55]](#cite_note-PP-57) The French embassy's walls and gates were set ablaze and damaged while Nigerien soldiers and General [Salifou Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salifou_Modi "Salifou Modi") were seen on the ground urging the crowds to disperse peacefully.[[50]](#cite_note-RF-52) The crowd left after police fired volleys of tear gas in response.[[51]](#cite_note-Balima-53) Images showed people being loaded into ambulances with bloodied legs.[[51]](#cite_note-Balima-53)

In response to the attack on its embassy, the [French government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_government "French government") warned that attacks on its nationals, military personnel, diplomats and interests would lead to an immediate and intractable response.[[58]](#cite_note-60)

On the behest of ECOWAS, [Chad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad "Chad")'s president [Mahamat Déby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahamat_D%C3%A9by "Mahamat Déby") met with Tchiani and Bazoum at the presidential palace in Niamey. The Chadian Presidency released pictures of the meeting, marking Bazoum's first appearance since the coup.[[59]](#cite_note-61) Meanwhile, Colonel Abdremane accused Hassoumi Massaoudou, still claiming to be acting leader substituting for Bazoum, of authorizing a French attack on the presidential palace to liberate Bazoum.[[60]](#cite_note-62) The [French Foreign Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Foreign_Ministry "French Foreign Ministry") denied there were any such plans.[[61]](#cite_note-63)

Bazoum's oil minister Mahamane Sani Mahamadou (son of former president [Mahamadou Issoufou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahamadou_Issoufou "Mahamadou Issoufou")), mining minister Ousseini Hadizatou and the head of the [PNDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerien_Party_for_Democracy_and_Socialism "Nigerien Party for Democracy and Socialism") national executive committee, [Foumakoye Gado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foumakoye_Gado "Foumakoye Gado") were arrested by the military junta. This followed the arrests of Transport Minister Oumarou Malam Alma and former defense minister Kalla Moutari the previous week.[[62]](#cite_note-64)[[63]](#cite_note-65)

Military chiefs of ECOWAS member states met in Abuja, to discuss the situation in Niger.[[68]](#cite_note-70) At the same time, a confidential military signal was picked up by Inside Nigeria, giving orders to the Nigerian military to name units for a military operation against Niger, mobilize the armed forces and establish a no-fly zone.[[69]](#cite_note-71) Hours later, [Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast") issued a statement in which it supported the ECOWAS sanctions and announced the country's participation in a preparation for a military intervention in Niger.[[70]](#cite_note-72)

A delegation of the Nigerien military junta headed by General Salifou Mody traveled to [Bamako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamako "Bamako"), Mali,[[71]](#cite_note-73) and then to [Ouagadougou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouagadougou "Ouagadougou"), Burkina Faso.[[72]](#cite_note-74) Speculation arose as to whether they went to ask for the support of the Wagner Group, which has a presence in Mali.[[73]](#cite_note-75)

**Betta Chimaobim Edu** (born 27 October 1986)[[2]](#cite_note-punchng-2) is a Nigerian medical doctor and politician. In 2015, Edu became the youngest person to be appointed Special Adviser to the Executive Governor of Cross River State [Benedict Ayade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Ayade "Benedict Ayade") on Community and Primary Healthcare.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

However, the APC's electoral performance and party unity were more mixed as it came a distant third in the [2021 Anambra State gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Anambra_State_gubernatorial_election "2021 Anambra State gubernatorial election")[[b]](#cite_note-APCprimary-43) and was still beset by infighting.[[42]](#cite_note-44) The APC primary was framed in the wider context of internal party feuds stemming from the APC's formation in 2013 and pre-[2019 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Nigerian_general_election "2019 Nigerian general election") party crises to the 2020 removal of party leadership and contentious 2021 state party congresses. The ability of the APC national caretaker committee to resolve state party factionizations and properly organize the 2022 national party convention was seen as vital for both the APC's presidential chances and its future as a party.[[43]](#cite_note-45) After several postponements, the convention was successfully held on 26 March 2022 despite some controversy over the consensus method used for most party offices.[[44]](#cite_note-46)[[45]](#cite_note-47)

Former Governor of Lagos State Bola Ahmed Tinubu emerged as the winner of Nigeria’s closely watched February 2023 presidential election. Despite [repeated calls](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/02/06/nigeria-impunity-insecurity-threaten-elections) to Nigerian authorities to prioritize accountability for [past elections-related abuses](https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/06/10/nigeria-widespread-violence-ushers-presidents-new-term) and address [widespread insecurity](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/08/09/nigeria-insecurity-grips-nations-capital), the February elections were blighted by incidents of logistical failures and violence at the polls.

Multiple armed groups continue to kill and jeopardize the livelihood of millions across the country. In the Northwest, gangs of so-called bandits carry out widespread killings, kidnappings, sexual violence, and lootings, while in the Northeast, there has been a resurgence of attacks by the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), a breakout faction of Boko Haram.

Decades long intercommunal conflict between farmers and herders in the Middle Belt and Northcentral region continue to claim lives, while the authorities struggle to contain the clashes around land and other resources, which are exacerbated by ethnic and religious tensions.

In their responses to the security crisis across the country, security forces continue to be implicated in gross human rights abuses, including indiscriminate airstrikes, while the authorities have repeatedly failed to hold officers responsible for the abuses accountable through the justice system.

High rates of inflation due to the removal of a subsidy on petrol, among other factors, gave rise to an increase in multidimensional poverty and economic inequality. The high inflation rate undermined access to food and other necessities in a country where millions live in extreme poverty without a functional social protection system.

According to the Center for Democracy and Development, a nongovernmental organization (NGO), [a total of 109 election-related deaths were recorded across Nigeria in the build-up to the 2023 general election](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/top-news/588325-nigeria-recorded-109-deaths-in-three-months-linked-to-2023-elections-cdd.html)s.

The presidential and federal legislative elections [recorded several incidences of violence at the polls](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/02/27/nigerias-elections-remain-risky-many-citizens), especially in battleground states like Lagos. In some cases, voters were injured and stripped of their right to vote without any intervention from security forces.

In April, [at least 80 people](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/gunmen-kidnap-80-including-children-northwest-nigeria-2023-04-08/), mostly women and children, were kidnapped by bandit gangs in Zamfara State. ## Boko Haram Conflict

Communities in Borno State, the epicenter of the Boko Haram conflict, witnessed a resurgence in attacks and kidnappings by armed groups. In March, over [30 fishermen and farmers were gruesomely killed](https://sunnewsonline.com/the-killing-of-30-borno-fishermen/) in an attack in Ngala Local Government Area. In June, [about 36 people](https://dailytrust.com/farmers-on-the-run-as-b-haram-killings-return/), including farmers, were killed in Dambo, Jere, and Mafa Local Government Areas.

According to [a media report](https://dailytrust.com/farmers-on-the-run-as-b-haram-killings-return/), ISWAP, a prominent breakout faction of Boko Haram, imposed a ban on farming, fishing, and herding activities in Marte Local Government Area. The move to halt agricultural activities was apparently to punish the farming communities for spying on them for the military, which carried out aerial bombardment against ISWAP.

## Abuses by Security Forces

In January, an [erroneous military airstrike in Nasarawa State](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/06/06/nigeria-no-justice-civilians-killed-airstrike) killed 39 people and injured 6 others. Since 2017, [over 300 people are reported to have been killed by airstrikes](https://www.sbmintel.com/2023/02/chart-of-the-week-nigeria-air-force-mishaps/) that the Nigerian air force claimed were intended for bandits or members of Boko Haram and its breakout factions but instead hit civilians. In 2022, [the Nigerian air force announced an investigation into accidental airstrikes on civilian](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/562027-were-investigating-accidental-airstrikes-on-civilians-nigerian-air-force-chief.html)s but provided no further details.

In July, anti-police brutality [protests erupted in Anambra State, following the death of Chidubem Ezenwa in](https://businessday.ng/columnist/article/the-police-could-trigger-another-unrest-in-nigeria/) [police custody](https://dailypost.ng/2023/08/06/anambra-family-agonizes-over-sons-death-in-police-custody/), after allegedly being beaten by police operatives and other inmates. [Police said](https://dailypost.ng/2023/08/06/anambra-family-agonizes-over-sons-death-in-police-custody/) the inmates who beat him up have been arraigned for murder.

## Accountability for Serious Crimes

In February, the National Human Rights Commission began an investigation into allegations of [forced abortions](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/nigeria-military-abortions/) and [infanticide](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/nigeria-military-children/) in the Northeast Boko Haram conflict, but it has yet to produce its findings.

Domestic trials for hundreds of Boko Haram suspects have remained postponed since 2018.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Office of the Prosecutor continued to consider whether to open an investigation into serious crimes committed in Nigeria and [indicated plans](https://asp.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/asp_docs/ICC-ASP-22-10-ENG-PPB-2024-31jul23-1500.pdf) to decide in 2024.

## Freedom of Expression and Media

In May, a Nigerian Court [found](https://punchng.com/just-in-nbc-has-no-powers-to-fine-broadcast-stations-court-rules/) that the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC), the country’s broadcast regulator, has no power to impose fines on broadcast stations. Nigerian naira (about US$6,500) for allegedly violating the NBC code in a program during which a vice presidential candidate called on the authorities not to swear in Bola Tinubu.

Although the Nigerian Constitution guarantees the right to freedom of expression, thought, and conscience, insult to religion remains a criminal offense and Sharia (Islamic law), applicable in 12 northern states, criminalizes blasphemy.

geria. In June, [Usman Buda was attacked and killed by a mob](https://dailytrust.com/how-sokoto-famous-butcher-was-killed-over-alleged-blasphemy/) in Sokoto State for alleged blasphemy against the Prophet Mohammed.

## Poverty and Inequality

President Tinubu announced the [removal of an existing subsidy on fuel](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-65737846) during his inauguration in May, resulting in increases in the price of food and other basic necessities. The authorities did not put in any measures to cushion the impact of the petrol subsidy removal, leaving [many Nigerians struggling to meet the basic needs of themselves and their families](https://www.theafricareport.com/316288/nigeria-petrol-price-hike-fuels-suffering/).

[The ability of communities to fish and farm continues to be stunted by rampant oil spills](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/feb/02/nearly-14000-nigerians-take-shell-to-court-over-devastating-impact-of-pollution) while the costs to public health is worsened by oil pollution and the [ongoing practice of excessive gas flaring.](https://blogs.worldbank.org/developmenttalk/impact-gas-flaring-child-health-nigeria)

In August, President Tinubu announced a [$650 million package](https://www.voanews.com/a/nigeria-s-tinubu-announces-650-million-aid-package-after-subsidy-removal-/7207196.html) that included funds to allow for a review of the minimum wage; support for small and medium businesses; and the purchase of gas-powered buses to reduce the cost of transportation, among other things.

## Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

In August, police in Delta State arrested dozens for [allegedly participating in a gay wedding](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/08/30/nigerian-police-arrest-dozens-alleged-gay-wedding) at a hotel. The police streamed on Facebook a public parade of the detainees in front of journalists, where they were interrogated regarding the accusations in violation of their rights to fair trial, dignity, and privacy.

A total of [69 people were remanded to prison](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/nigerian-court-remands-dozens-prison-over-alleged-gay-wedding-2023-09-04/) in connection with the incident and later [released on bail pending trial.](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/nigerian-court-frees-bail-dozens-arrested-over-alleged-gay-wedding-lawyer-2023-09-19/#:~:text=A%20court%20sitting%20in%20southern,court%2C%20lawyer%20Ochuko%20Ohimor%20said.)

In October, [76 people were arrested in Gombe State for allegedly attending a birthday party for gay people](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/10/24/africa/nigeria-paramilitary-raids-gay-party-intl/index.html). The arrests were conducted by the Nigerian Security and Civil Defense Corps, the country’s paramilitary agency, which also alleged that the organizers of the party planned to hold a same-sex wedding.

The [Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act](https://www.refworld.org/pdfid/52f4d9cc4.pdf), 2013, punishes same-sex marriage and public displays of same-sex relationships with 14 and 10 years’ imprisonment, respectively. It also punishes establishing, supporting, and participating in gay organizations with 10 years in prison.

A 2016 Human Rights Watch [report](https://www.hrw.org/report/2016/10/20/tell-me-where-i-can-be-safe/impact-nigerias-same-sex-marriage-prohibition-act) found that, despite no evidence that anyone had been prosecuted or sentenced under the law by that time, the law had served to legitimize abuses against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people in Nigeria, including extortion, arbitrary arrest, torture, and physical and sexual violence.

The police used the law for the first time in 2019 to [prosecute 47 men accused of same-sex public displays of affection](https://www.cnn.com/2019/12/12/africa/nigeria-men-trial-anti-gay-law-intl/index.html) in Lagos State. A court [dismissed](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/27/world/africa/Nigeria-anti-gay-law.html) the case because the police failed to appear and present witnesses.

## Disability Rights

In January, then-President Muhammadu Buhari signed the Mental Health Bill into law, replacing the 1958 Lunacy Act. The new bill established some protections for people with mental health conditions, including the right to participate in their treatment plans. It also imposes a ban on chaining people with mental health conditions and aims to expand community-based coverage so more people can access mental health services. Contrary to international human rights standards, the law continues to permit involuntary treatment and allows coercion in other forms, including restraints and seclusion.

The latest measures announced by the president include allocations for a review of the minimum wage, support for micro-, small- and medium-scale enterprises, and the purchase of 3,000 gas-powered buses to reduce the cost of transportation.

Tinubu also ordered the immediate release of 200,000 metric tons of grains to households, in an effort to lower prices, and 225,000 metric tons of fertilizers, seedlings and other inputs to farmers.

"I had promised to reform the economy for the long-term good by fighting major imbalances that have plagued our economy," Tinubu said. "Ending the subsidy and preferential exchange rate system were key to this fight. This fight is to define the fate and future of our nation."

Upon assuming office in late May, Tinubu embarked on some of Nigeria's biggest reforms in decades, including floating of the country's currency, the naira.

Fuel prices have more than tripled since the subsidy removal and the currency has weakened against the U.S. dollar. The developments increased pressure on the government to ease the suffering caused by the policies.

Authorities say the decision will pay off in the long run. On Monday, Tinubu said the country has saved $1.32 billion since scrapping the subsidy in late May.

"Such a vast sum of money would have been better spent on public transportation, health care, schools, housing and even national security," he said.

But economist Isaac Botti said authorities should have implemented measures in advance to cushion the effect of removing the subsidy.

"What the government ought to have done was to create the shock absorber, but trying to salvage a crisis after it has occurred for me is an afterthought," Botti said. "So what the president expressed in his speech were things he should have done or should have been out in place before the pronouncement of subsidy removal."

Botti said Nigeria needs to consider local refining of oil if it is going to bring down soaring fuel prices.

"What is the plan [including] short, medium and long term to address the issue of refining petrol in this country? Whatever measures the government is bringing on board should be able to address the realities on ground," he said.

Last month, Tinubu announced plans to transfer $10 million to $12 million to poor households in a bid to ease the impact of the subsidy removal.

## Ending the fuel subsidy

This challenge has been kicked down the road by successive governments since its introduction in the 1970s.

(Abuja) – The failure of the [Nigerian](https://www.hrw.org/africa/nigeria) authorities to address accountability for past elections-related abuses and widespread insecurity across the country threaten the safe conduct of the upcoming 2023 general elections, Human Rights Watch said today.

On February 25, Nigerians will elect a new president to replace President Muhammadu Buhari, who is completing his second 4-year consecutive term, the maximum allowed. They will elect federal National Assembly members the same day and governors and state lawmakers on March 11.

“There is a thick veil of violence shrouding the 2023 elections that undermines people’s fundamental right to vote,” said [Anietie Ewang](https://www.hrw.org/about/people/anietie-ewang), Nigeria researcher at Human Rights Watch. “It is important for the authorities to swiftly restore public confidence in their ability to hold those responsible for electoral violence accountable and ensure the safety and security of all Nigerians.”

The elections are set to take place against a backdrop of impunity for abuses by security forces and other actors during the previous general elections in 2019. There have also been [security threats from multiple groups](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/08/09/nigeria-insecurity-grips-nations-capital) across the country, including violent gangs in the northwest and groups in southeastern Nigeria who have been trying to undermine the elections.

Nigeria’s elections have historically been fraught with violence and other abuses. The election of President Buhari in 2015, the first transition of power to an opposition party since the country’s democratic transition in 1999, was largely peaceful. But the 2019 election was [marred by violence from security forces](https://www.thisdaylive.com/index.php/2019/03/11/international-observers-condemn-violence-military-involvement-in-nigerian-elections/), including the army, and thugs acting on behalf of politicians.

Human Rights Watch [research on the 2019 elections](https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/06/10/nigeria-widespread-violence-ushers-presidents-new-term) in Rivers state in the south and Kano in the north, both of which have a strong history of violent elections, found that pre-election tensions including clashes between supporters of major political parties and rivalry between key politicians culminated in serious violence during the elections. Military officials indiscriminately shot and killed civilians in Rivers state while political thugs and security officials attacked election officials, voters, journalists, and other observers in both states.

Under international human rights law, federal and local officials are required to take all reasonable steps to create and maintain an environment in which election officials, journalists, and civil society can operate free from violence and intimidation. Democratic elections require the protection of freedom of expression and access to information. The United Nations special rapporteur on the right to freedom of opinion and expression has issued [detailed guidance](https://icj2.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/Report-SRFoE-2014-eng.pdf)on how to ensure freedom of opinion, expression, and access to information during elections.

Despite repeated calls to the Nigerian authorities to ensure justice and accountability for election-related violence, Human Rights Watch has found that there has been little progress. A [committee set up by the Nigerian Army](https://army.mil.ng/?p=3017) to investigate allegations of violence and killings against officers during the elections was given two weeks in March 2019 to produce its findings. Four years later, the authorities have provided no information on the committee’s work, findings, or recommendations.

In 2020, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) [announced the prosecution](https://punchng.com/2019-polls-18-offenders-facing-trial-in-seven-states-inec/) of 18 people in seven states across the country for offenses during the 2019 elections, including snatching and destroying election materials, disorderly conduct, unlawful possession of ballot papers and Permanent Voters’ Cards, and vote buying at polling places on election day. It is unclear how many of these cases have concluded or led to convictions.

The commission indicated that it faces [constraints in ensuring justice and accountability for electoral offenses](https://www.thisdaylive.com/index.php/2022/12/04/inec-explains-inability-to-prosecute-electoral-offenders/) because, while it can prosecute offenders, the authority to investigate rests with the security agencies. This has led to a lack of effectiveness in dealing with cases involving election infractions, the commission said.
